text: A talk is a good way to explain some concept. When doing a talk you need to know your audience, you can't target beginners and advanced users at once A failed talk can happen for many reason - wrong subject - bad slides/content - wrong audience targeting Substack There are no hard subjects to be cover in a presentation, there are only different ways of presenting them. I did a “bad” talk at Rancho Dev when I’ve talked about Forms and Formik (slides and code here). The problem of this talk was about my assumptions of the audience. I’m used to talking in places that most people know basic React concepts, but Rancho Dev conf was a more broad conferences with many different topics. As I did not provide more context (a basic intro of React, react hooks and so on), it was hard to explain to them how to apply this concepts to solve the forms in React land. I always ask for feedback ( give me here) after my talk, and this one I received a really bad one saying that I thought the audience won’t grasp the concepts. The truth was that I didn’t understand really well these concepts to explain like I’m 5. How would be a better talk for that audience? - More about the problem and motivation (how hard complex forms can be to get right) - basic React intro concepts - more concepts less code Link Community you need to give talk to create a community Share

text: When I come back to São Paulo to make my internship at PontoTel Startup. I could live in my parents house at Guarulhs for "free" It would only take me 2 hours to go to work and 2 hours to go back home. I would lose 4 hours per day commuting, 20 hours per week and 80 hours per month. That's 960 hours per year. I knew that my time was my precious resource, so I decided to buy it. If you do basic math, I work 8 hours per day, 5 days per week, 4 weeks per month, that's 160 hours per month. I was earning R$1500.00, so my hour was R$9.35. I was losing 80 hours R$9.35 = R$748 per month. I found a room to rent in São Paulo for R$400.00 and used these extra 4 hours to study and work a lot. All these 4 hours paid off a lot. I was able to work more, study more and learn more. I was also going to happy hours and networking events, which helped me to meet a lot of people. Additionally, I was able to create a tech community and find my co-founder for my own Startup.

text: Your first solution for a problem won’t be the best one. The first thing you need to do when trying to solve a problem is to research for existing solutions for the given problem. Most of the time someone else already solved your problem or a similar one. After having a list of possible solutions you should evaluate them using some criteria. A problem always has more than one solution. Finding the best solution is an optimization problem where you use some criteria to evaluate the score of your solution. You can have some requirements that you should meet eliminating a few possible solutions. After finding the minimal set of possible solutions you need to try all of them in small proof of concepts to understanding their tradeoffs in practice. The simplest solution should be preferred. If you want to use this solution in a production system with a team, you have some more steps to follow. You need to ensure you can deliver this solution incrementally without breaking anything. You also need to write a RFC and demo your solution to your team, to make sure everybody is onboard. Other people can find problems in your proposed solution and edge cases that you have not thought about it, making you need to reevaluate your approach. Summary Finding the best solution for a given problem takes sometime as you need to evaluate many options before deciding. Picking the first one or the “best practice” or most used solution could not be the best solution for your problem and requirements.

text: After Tobi talking about there is not such thing as frontend engineer and that you need to know more layers I'd like to talk about all the layers that I've learning in college Some people think that college is a waste of money and time for computer science. I think we can go from electrons to no-code to cover all layers and abstractions that you need to know, not master, to understand what it is really going on. The basic building blocks of a CPU is the transistor. A transistor let electric current pass given a following configuration. So we have 0 and 1, binary. 0 is no current and 1 is current. And everything is built on top of this concept. Then we have boolean logic, that let us sum, subtract and to most math using binary code. We use logic ports to create basic arithmetic. If you add PC (program counter), a clock, you have a basic CPU. If you can load data from memory and write to memory, you can do anything your modern computer does. You can build your own assembly, then you decode each instructions and execute simple programs. After that you could keep using assembly, or build a higher level language to compile to assembly to make your life easier, like C.

My advice here is to focus more on solving problems. And solving a new problem usually is a combination of solving some existing problem that you already solved, some problems that you don't know how to solve, and some knowledge and experience that you have and some that you are missing. Most of the time you should focus on breadth if you want to solve more kind of problems. You focus in learning few about a lot of things. If you want to solve better a kind of problem you need to go in depth. You focus in learning a lot about a few things. You need to balance these approaches. I usually only go deep when my current knowldge/experience is not enough to solve the problem that I have to solve.
